paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships requires deciding which interventions will reveal useful information about a system. This paper focuses on making those experiments more data efficient. It treats causal discovery as an online learning problem, where the choice of the next intervention depends on what previous observations have already revealed.

The method selects interventions from a graph separating system: a collection that cuts every graph edge at least once. Such a collection is sufficient to identify the causal graph with unlimited interventional data. The proposed track-and-stop algorithm addresses finite sampling by adaptively allocating experiments, updating its graph estimate from the accumulated history, and stopping when a condition tied to the requested confidence is satisfied.

The authors establish a problem-dependent upper bound on the expected number of intervention samples. In simulations with randomly generated causal graphs, the method achieves better structural accuracy with substantially fewer samples than existing methods. These results support adapting both experimental allocation and stopping to the evidence gathered.
icml-2024-adaptive-online-experimental-d.tldr: An adaptive causal discovery algorithm chooses interventions and a stopping point to learn causal graphs with fewer experimental samples.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo generates samples from complicated probability distributions by repeatedly moving between states. The rules governing those moves strongly influence how efficiently the chain explores the distribution. This paper proposes learning those transition rules, with the aim of obtaining efficient sampling and good mixing rather than specifying every aspect of the sampler manually.

The training objective minimizes total variation distance between the chain's stationary distribution and the empirical data distribution. The method builds involutive Metropolis-Hastings kernels from reversible neural networks. These constructions ensure detailed balance by design, embedding an important mathematical property of the sampler directly into its architecture.

Reversibility also has consequences for the adversarial training component. The authors show that it implies a C2 symmetry requirement for the discriminator, allowing its possible functions to be restricted accordingly. The contribution therefore connects learned sampling with structural guarantees: reversibility shapes both the transition mechanism and the discriminator used to train it.
icml-2024-ai-sampler-adversarial-learnin.tldr: Ai-sampler learns Markov chain transitions using reversible neural networks that enforce detailed balance and constrain adversarial training.

paragraphs: Interior-point methods are best known for convex optimization, where barriers help an algorithm handle constraints while searching within the feasible region. This paper establishes favorable theoretical complexity for a broader setting: optimizing a non-convex objective subject to general convex set constraints and linear constraints. The non-convexity is therefore in the optimization problem without requiring arbitrary non-convex constraint sets.

The authors propose first-order and second-order methods based on self-concordant barriers. Their targets are suitably defined approximate Karush-Kuhn-Tucker points, which express approximate stationarity under constraints. This distinction matters because reaching such a point is a different achievement from proving that the globally best solution has been found.

For accuracy tolerance epsilon, the worst-case iteration bounds are O(epsilon^-2) for the first-order method and O(epsilon^-3/2) for the second-order method. These rates are similar to those for unconstrained problems. The result shows that, within the paper's formulation, incorporating these constraints through barriers can preserve favorable iteration complexity beyond the usual convex setting.
icml-2024-barrier-algorithms-for-constra.tldr: Barrier-based methods reach approximate constrained stationarity in non-convex problems with iteration rates similar to unconstrained optimization.

paragraphs: Generative document retrieval assigns each document an index and trains an autoregressive neural model to produce the appropriate index from a query. This paper asks how the choice of those indexes affects retrieval. Its central idea is that an index is an information channel whose design can constrain what the retrieval system communicates.

The authors reformulate retrieval using information theory, treating indexes as a bottleneck between documents and queries. Shannon's rate-distortion theory provides a way to analyze indexing quality through mutual information. This perspective makes index design part of the retrieval problem itself, rather than treating document identifiers as an incidental representation chosen before learning begins.

The paper empirically quantifies this bottleneck and proposes a bottleneck-minimal indexing method. Evaluations on NQ320K and MARCO show that the proposed method outperforms the previous indexing methods included in the comparison. The findings support the practical value of analyzing how much useful information passes through indexes when designing generative retrieval systems.
icml-2024-bottleneck-minimal-indexing-fo.tldr: An information-theoretic approach to document indexes improves generative retrieval over the indexing methods evaluated on NQ320K and MARCO.

paragraphs: Many selection problems involve choosing a limited number of items whose combined value exhibits diminishing returns. Monotone submodular maximization captures this structure, with a cardinality constraint limiting the number selected. This paper studies what happens when items arrive over time and the selected set must remain useful without changing too much after each arrival.

The authors make stability an explicit requirement by bounding the number of changes between consecutive solutions. At the same time, the maintained solution should achieve a constant approximation to the best available selection. These two objectives create a trade-off: the algorithm must respond to new opportunities while respecting a limit on how much it revises its choices.

The paper provides algorithms with different balances between approximation quality and consistency. It also evaluates them on real-world instances, reporting evidence of their effectiveness. The contribution is a framework for maintaining valuable selections in a stream while treating the disruption caused by updates as part of the optimization problem.
icml-2024-consistent-submodular-maximiza.tldr: The paper develops streaming selection algorithms that trade off solution quality against how much the selected set changes.

paragraphs: DE-COP investigates whether a language model was trained on particular copyrighted text when its training collection is undisclosed. The method starts from the premise that a model is likely to recognize exact passages it encountered during training. It turns that premise into a recognition task rather than relying solely on access to internal model outputs.

The model receives multiple-choice questions containing an original excerpt alongside paraphrased versions. To evaluate this approach, the authors build BookTection, which contains excerpts and paraphrases from 165 books published before and after a model's training cutoff. The evaluation thus connects recognition behavior with books whose publication timing differs relative to training.

For models exposing logits, the authors report an 8.6% improvement over the prior best method on the AUC detection measure. For fully black-box models, they report 72% average accuracy in detecting suspect books, compared with approximately 0% for prior methods. These experimental findings support recognition-based probing as a useful approach under restricted model access.
icml-2024-de-cop-detecting-copyrighted-c.tldr: DE-COP probes whether models recognize original book excerpts among paraphrases to detect possible training-data inclusion.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks approximate solutions to partial differential equations, but checking their outputs at selected points leaves gaps between those checks. A model could behave substantially worse elsewhere in its space-and-time domain. This paper addresses that gap by seeking guarantees on worst-case residual error throughout the continuous domain where the model is intended to apply.

The authors establish error-based conditions and introduce partial-CROWN, a framework that bounds residual errors after a network has been trained. Residual error measures how closely the network satisfies the governing equation. Certifying that quantity across a domain gives a different form of evidence from comparing predictions with a numerical solver at a finite collection of inputs.

The framework is presented as general, efficient, and scalable. The authors demonstrate tight certificates for networks associated with Burgers', Schrödinger's, Allan-Cahn, and Diffusion-Sorption equations. These results show how post-training certification can strengthen the evidence available for a physics-informed network by bounding equation violations beyond individually tested locations.
icml-2024-efficient-error-certification-.tldr: Partial-CROWN certifies bounds on physics-informed neural networks' residual errors across continuous domains after training.

paragraphs: Human feedback can help improve language models, but the usefulness of that feedback depends partly on which questions are asked. This paper studies an agent that gathers feedback sequentially while learning a reward model. Each round provides evidence that can influence subsequent queries, making feedback collection an exploration problem rather than a fixed sequence of requests.

The strongest agent in the experiments combines double Thompson sampling for query generation with an epistemic neural network for representing uncertainty. These components address related decisions: what the reward model remains unsure about, and how that uncertainty should guide the next query. The study examines both as parts of an effective feedback-gathering process.

The experiments show that efficient exploration can reach high performance using far fewer queries. They also indicate that uncertainty estimation and the exploration scheme each play critical roles. The practical message is that feedback efficiency depends on the strategy for acquiring information as well as the model that learns from the resulting responses.
icml-2024-efficient-exploration-for-llms.tldr: Experiments show that uncertainty-aware exploration can substantially reduce the human-feedback queries needed to improve language models.

paragraphs: Iterative neural networks repeatedly feed their own outputs back into the model to refine a prediction. This paper identifies another use for that sequence of outputs: estimating uncertainty. The authors argue that the rate at which successive predictions converge is strongly correlated with the accuracy of the prediction they eventually approach.

Their method uses this convergence behavior as a proxy for uncertainty. Because an iterative model already produces successive outputs, the approach can draw on its existing computation without modifying the original model. The uncertainty signal is therefore connected to how the prediction develops during refinement, rather than requiring a separate collection of models.

The authors report state-of-the-art uncertainty estimates at substantially lower computational cost than approaches such as ensembles. They demonstrate practical value in road detection from aerial imagery and in estimating aerodynamic properties of two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes. The findings support convergence rate as a useful empirical indicator of prediction reliability in the iterative networks studied.
icml-2024-enabling-uncertainty-estimatio.tldr: The convergence rate of an iterative network's predictions provides an inexpensive uncertainty signal without changing the model.

paragraphs: Canonicalization and frame averaging offer ways to enforce symmetry without designing a specialized equivariant architecture. They use transformations of an input to build a symmetry-respecting function. This paper examines whether that process also preserves continuity, so that small input changes do not produce abrupt output changes.

The authors establish a theoretical obstruction for commonly used groups: no efficiently computable choice of unweighted frame preserves continuity in the setting studied. As a result, averaging can transform a smooth function without symmetry into a symmetric function with discontinuities. This gives a theoretical explanation for empirical benefits previously observed with probabilistic frames that weight different group elements.

To address the problem, the paper formally defines weighted frames and constructs examples that provably preserve continuity. It supplies efficient, continuous weighted frames for the actions of SO(d), O(d), and S_n on point clouds. The contribution makes continuity an explicit design requirement alongside symmetry and shows how weighting can satisfy that requirement in these cases.
icml-2024-equivariant-frames-and-the-imp.tldr: The paper identifies continuity barriers for unweighted frame averaging and constructs weighted frames that preserve continuity for point-cloud symmetries.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback can work well with relatively little feedback, but explaining that efficiency theoretically remains challenging. This paper studies policy optimization, addressing a gap between its empirical success and a literature largely focused on value-based algorithms. The goal is to understand how an agent can learn effectively when rewards are inferred from human comparisons.

The proposed PO-RLHF algorithm builds on Policy Cover-Policy Gradient, which assumes access to the reward function. Here, the agent instead learns about rewards through comparisons between trajectories. The authors develop a trajectory-level elliptical potential analysis to infer reward parameters from these comparisons, adapting the analysis to feedback that does not directly reveal reward values.

The paper provides performance bounds with low query complexity and analyzes versions using linear and neural function approximation. These bounds offer theoretical insight into why a small amount of human feedback may suffice for good RLHF performance. The result concerns the analyzed algorithms and settings, preserving the distinction between that explanation and a universal claim about feedback requirements.
icml-2024-exploration-driven-policy-opti.tldr: The paper gives low-query performance bounds for policy-based RLHF that learns rewards from comparisons between trajectories.

paragraphs: Running large language models on end-user devices motivates compression to very small storage budgets. This paper targets extreme quantization, including representations using only two to three bits per parameter. Its method, AQLM, adapts additive quantization from information retrieval to compress language-model weights while retaining useful predictive accuracy.

AQLM introduces two main changes to the classic approach. It learns additive representations of weight matrices in a way that adapts to their inputs, and it jointly optimizes codebook parameters within each transformer block. The method therefore coordinates the compressed representation across a block instead of treating its codebook parameters as entirely independent choices.

The authors report a Pareto-optimal accuracy-versus-size trade-off below three bits per parameter and substantial improvements over known schemes in the two-bit regime. They also provide CPU and GPU implementations for token generation that match or exceed optimized FP16 speed while using much less memory. These results connect compression quality with practical execution, showing that the representation can support efficient inference as well as smaller storage.
icml-2024-extreme-compression-of-large-l.tldr: AQLM uses learned additive quantization to improve extreme LLM compression while supporting fast CPU and GPU token generation.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed stochastic differential equations serve as mathematical proxies for stochastic optimization algorithms. This paper studies what these models imply about generalization: how performance on training data relates to performance beyond it. Earlier analyses supplied either bounds in expectation or bounds containing information-theoretic quantities that could not be computed.

The authors prove high-probability generalization bounds without nontrivial information-theoretic terms. Their proof technique estimates entropy flows associated with the fractional Fokker-Planck equation, which describes how the probability distribution of the heavy-tailed process evolves. This connects distributional dynamics to guarantees that hold with high probability, rather than describing only an average across outcomes.

The resulting bounds also improve the dependence on parameter dimension relative to prior work. A further finding is a phase transition suggesting that heavy tails may help or hurt depending on the problem's structure. Experiments across several settings support the theory. The analysis therefore offers a more qualified account of heavy-tailed behavior than a blanket claim that it always improves generalization.
icml-2024-generalization-bounds-for-heav.tldr: New high-probability bounds clarify how heavy-tailed optimization proxies generalize and suggest that heavy tails can help or hurt depending on problem structure.

paragraphs: Private clustering aims to group data while protecting information about the individuals represented in it. Researchers have developed different algorithms for centralized, local, and shuffle models of differential privacy. This paper asks whether those separate lines of work can be brought together through a shared algorithmic approach while keeping clustering error competitive.

The authors show that a small modification to an algorithm developed twenty years earlier can make it work across these privacy models. Reusing one underlying method provides a unified account of a landscape that otherwise contains many distinct algorithms. Its significance lies in covering multiple privacy settings while retaining strong results within them.

The approach matches almost all previously known results and improves some of them. It also extends to continual observation, where the input changes over time and a new clustering solution must be released at every time step. This extension brings repeated, evolving outputs into the same broader framework, rather than limiting the contribution to a single clustering of static data.
icml-2024-making-old-things-new-a-unifie.tldr: A lightly modified older algorithm unifies several private clustering settings, matches most prior results, and extends to continually changing data.

paragraphs: Time-series datasets often combine channels measured at different rates, making it difficult to learn a useful shared representation without labels. The paper motivates this problem with financial information collected daily, monthly, or quarterly. MF-CLR addresses these mixed frequencies through self-supervised contrastive learning, aiming to represent the channels together while accounting for their different sampling rates.

Its central mechanism is a hierarchy spanning frequencies along the feature dimension. Within each contrastive block, two groups of subseries at adjacent frequencies are embedded using a proposed cross-frequency consistency principle. This makes relationships between neighboring frequencies part of the representation-learning process, giving the method a structure tailored to multi-frequency data.

The authors evaluate the learned representations on long-term forecasting, short-term forecasting, classification, anomaly detection, and imputation. They report leading performance across these five tasks and consistent performance across target dataset sizes in transfer learning experiments. The findings support the usefulness of the representation across several distinct downstream uses, rather than only one forecasting setup.
icml-2024-mf-clr-multi-frequency-contras.tldr: MF-CLR learns representations of differently sampled time-series channels through hierarchical contrastive learning across frequencies.

paragraphs: Serving several language models efficiently is difficult when their popularity differs. Resource allocation must account for how much demand each model receives as well as the resources its requests consume. MuxServe addresses this problem by coordinating the placement and execution of multiple models so that memory and computation can be shared more effectively.

The system uses model popularity to guide colocation for memory sharing. It also distinguishes the prefill and decoding phases of inference, separating and flexibly colocating them according to their computational characteristics. A placement algorithm, adaptive batch scheduling, and a unified resource manager implement this approach around a formal formulation of the multiplexing problem.

The evaluation reports up to 1.8 times higher throughput, or 2.9 times as many processed requests while attaining service-level objectives for 99% of requests. These are reported evaluation outcomes, with the throughput figure explicitly an upper result. They show the potential value of scheduling around both model demand and inference phase when operating multiple language-model endpoints.
icml-2024-muxserve-flexible-spatial-temp.tldr: MuxServe improves multi-LLM serving by coordinating model placement and scheduling around popularity, memory use, and inference phases.

paragraphs: A neural network's loss landscape describes how its training objective changes as its parameters change. Visualizations help researchers reason about that landscape and the training process, but reducing a high-dimensional object to a viewable form is difficult. This paper focuses on the limited flexibility and fidelity of linear visualization methods such as principal component analysis.

Neuro-Visualizer uses an autoencoder to construct a nonlinear landscape representation. The approach is intended to capture structure that a linear representation may miss, improving the usefulness of the resulting visualization. Its purpose is to provide a more faithful basis for inspecting neural-network behavior and interpreting claims about training.

The authors test the method on multiple problems within two applications of knowledge-guided machine learning. They report that it outperforms both linear and nonlinear baselines and produces insights that support some community claims while challenging others. The findings suggest that the choice of visualization method can affect the conclusions drawn from a loss landscape, making representation fidelity consequential for interpretation.
icml-2024-neuro-visualizer-a-novel-auto-.tldr: Neuro-Visualizer uses a nonlinear autoencoder representation to improve loss-landscape visualization and investigate claims about neural-network training.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability seeks directions in a transformer's internal activations that correspond to concepts used in its computations. Finding these feature vectors can require substantial labeled data. Observable propagation, or ObProp, proposes a way to identify task-relevant linear features using almost no data, reducing dependence on costly examples and annotations.

The method is organized around observables: linear functions associated with particular tasks. Alongside the procedure, the authors develop a mathematical theory for analyzing feature vectors. This includes a coupling coefficient that estimates how strongly the output of one feature correlates with that of another, providing a way to compare features through their behavior.

The paper applies ObProp in qualitative investigations of gendered occupational bias, political party prediction, and programming-language detection. The results suggest that it surpasses traditional feature-finding methods when data are scarce. They also suggest that the approach can help explain mechanisms behind language-model bias. These findings position ObProp as a tool for examining task-related internal computations with limited labeled evidence.
icml-2024-observable-propagation-uncover.tldr: ObProp finds task-relevant transformer feature vectors with almost no data and provides mathematical tools for comparing them.

paragraphs: Online filtering estimates a system's hidden state as measurements arrive. Outliers and inaccurate assumptions about the measurement process can make this difficult. This paper derives a Bayesian update rule designed to remain robust in the presence of both, while keeping the computation efficient enough for sequential use.

The approach combines generalized Bayesian inference with filtering methods such as the extended and ensemble Kalman filters. Generalized inference supplies the basis for the robustness result, while the filtering methods support efficient computation for nonlinear models. The resulting update has a closed form, bringing the theoretical robustness argument and the computational procedure into one method.

The authors evaluate the approach on object tracking, state estimation in high-dimensional chaotic systems, and online neural-network learning with outlier measurements. Across these experiments, it matches or outperforms other robust filters, including methods based on variational Bayes, at much lower computational cost. The findings show that robustness and efficient updating can be achieved together in the evaluated filtering problems.
icml-2024-outlier-robust-kalman-filterin.tldr: A closed-form generalized Bayesian update makes Kalman-style filtering robust to outliers while reducing computation in the evaluated problems.

paragraphs: Training and feedback data help determine what AI systems learn about human expectations. This position paper argues that collecting those data accurately is part of building models that are fair, trustworthy, and aligned with public interests. It identifies a gap between the importance of data collection and the limited training many AI researchers receive in collection methods.

The authors propose drawing on survey methodology, a field devoted to the science of collecting data. They summarize insights from that literature and discuss how those insights could improve training and feedback datasets. The argument connects data-centric AI's emphasis on data quality with an existing body of knowledge about how collection processes shape the information obtained.

The paper also proposes collaborative research on mitigating biases introduced during collection. Its contribution is a research position and a bridge between fields, rather than a new model or a reported performance benchmark. The intended direction is to improve accuracy and human-centered behavior by improving how evidence about people's expectations enters the training process.
icml-2024-position-insights-from-survey-.tldr: This position paper argues that survey methodology can improve AI training and feedback data by strengthening collection practices.

paragraphs: This position paper argues for responsible open sourcing of generative AI in the near and medium term. It places that argument within a debate about the technology's expected benefits, potential harms, and regulation. The authors support regulation while expressing concern that it could put the developing open-source ecosystem at risk.

To make the discussion more precise, the paper introduces a taxonomy of AI openness and applies it to forty large language models. This provides a structured way to discuss differences in openness. The authors then compare the benefits and risks of open and closed approaches, treating access arrangements as relevant to both opportunities and safety concerns.

The paper also presents potential mitigation measures, ranging from best practices to areas needing technical and scientific contributions. Its contribution is a framework and a policy position, with responsible release as the advocated direction. The argument aims to broaden public discussion of societal impacts while keeping the distinct benefits and risks of openness visible in decisions about generative AI.
icml-2024-position-near-to-mid-term-risk.tldr: The paper advocates responsible open-source generative AI, supported by an openness taxonomy and a comparison of benefits, risks, and mitigations.

paragraphs: AIM is a collection of vision models pretrained with an autoregressive objective inspired by language-model training. The paper investigates whether this approach produces visual representations that improve as training grows. Its focus is on the quality of the learned features and their usefulness for downstream tasks.

The authors report two scaling findings: visual-feature performance improves with both model capacity and data quantity, and the pretraining objective's value correlates with downstream performance. The second relationship matters because it connects the quantity optimized during pretraining to the practical usefulness of the resulting representation. The training procedure also scales without image-specific stabilization strategies.

As a large-scale demonstration, a seven-billion-parameter AIM trained on two billion images achieves 84.0% on ImageNet-1k while keeping its trunk frozen. The authors observe no performance saturation at the studied scale, suggesting potential for further scaling. This is evidence of continued improvement within their observations, with future gains presented as a possibility rather than an established outcome.
icml-2024-scalable-pre-training-of-large.tldr: AIM shows that autoregressive vision pretraining can yield stronger visual features as model size and training data increase.

paragraphs: Zero-shot quantization converts a pretrained full-precision network into a lower-precision model without access to its original training data. Synthetic data provide a substitute for that missing data. This paper asks how those synthetic examples should be generated when the goal includes improving the quantized model's generalization through lower sharpness.

The authors first establish, under certain assumptions, that sharpness minimization can be achieved by maximizing alignment between reconstruction-loss gradients on synthetic data and real validation data. Since real validation data are unavailable in the intended setting, they approximate that matching objective using gradients from each generated sample and its neighbors. The practical method thus replaces the inaccessible comparison with a synthetic-data-based one.

Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet show improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in low-bit quantization settings. The contribution is a criterion for generating data that explicitly considers the quantized model's sharpness. Its theoretical motivation is conditional, while the reported experiments provide evidence that the proposed approximation is useful in the evaluated compression settings.
icml-2024-sharpness-aware-data-generatio.tldr: Sharpness-aware synthetic data generation improves low-bit quantization without access to the model's original training data.

paragraphs: Time-series analysis requires recognizing both nearby relationships and patterns that span longer intervals. This paper introduces TSLANet, a lightweight convolutional model intended for multiple time-series tasks. It responds to concerns about Transformer-based models' noise sensitivity, computational efficiency, and tendency to overfit when datasets are small.

TSLANet combines an Adaptive Spectral Block with an Interactive Convolution Block. The spectral component uses Fourier analysis to represent long-term and short-term interactions, while adaptive thresholding mitigates noise. The convolutional component and self-supervised learning further support learning complex temporal patterns. Together, these elements give the model several ways to represent temporal structure and improve robustness across datasets.

The authors evaluate classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection, reporting performance above state-of-the-art models in the experiments. They also examine different noise levels and data sizes, finding resilience across those conditions. These results support the proposed architecture as a broadly useful time-series representation model within the evaluated settings, with spectral processing and convolution contributing to its design.
icml-2024-tslanet-rethinking-transformer.tldr: TSLANet combines adaptive spectral processing, convolution, and self-supervised learning for robust performance across several time-series tasks.

paragraphs: Producing nanomaterials with a desired shape and size remains a difficult experimental task. This paper explores whether AI can help predict nanoparticle morphology while working within constraints on available data. The question is practically motivated by demand for materials with specific forms, but the study is framed as an investigation of existing approaches' potential.

The authors first create a multimodal dataset that is twice the size of those in analogous studies. They then systematically evaluate classical machine-learning methods and large language models for predicting nanomaterial shapes and sizes. This connects a dataset contribution with a comparison of modeling approaches aimed at the same scientific prediction problem.

The study also develops a prototype text-to-image system, extending its exploration beyond shape and size prediction. The authors discuss the empirical results alongside the limitations and promise of the approaches examined. Taken together, the work provides a basis for assessing how different AI methods might support morphology prediction when data availability remains a central constraint.
icml-2024-unveiling-the-potential-of-ai-.tldr: The study builds a larger multimodal dataset and evaluates AI approaches for nanoparticle shape and size prediction under data constraints.
